sequences.title: Geometry: Every Shape Hides a Rectangle

screens.title: Area you already own
lines: You can already find a rectangle's area: base × height counts the unit squares hiding inside.
Today's secret: every triangle is HALF of some rectangle, and a parallelogram is a rectangle that leaned sideways — shear it back upright and not one square is lost.

vocab.meaning: the number of unit squares a shape covers (cm², m², …)
the straight-up distance from the base — never the slanted side

screens.framing: No grade, no pressure — just try something. Even a wild guess teaches your brain what to listen for.

screens.title: Every circle keeps the same secret
lines: Measure AROUND any circle (the circumference), measure ACROSS it (the diameter), then divide: you always get about 3.14 — for a teacup, a bike wheel, the moon. Every circle ever.
That forever-number is π (pi): C = π × d, and area A = π × r². In this realm we use π ≈ 3.14.

vocab.meaning: circumference ÷ diameter — always about 3.14, for every circle ever
the distance from the center to the edge: half the diameter

items.prompt: Amal cuts a rectangular brownie slab, 8 inches by 6 inches, along its diagonal into two matching triangles. What is the area of ONE triangle, in square inches?
items.hint: What's the area of the whole slab — and what does the diagonal do to it?
items.explanation: The slab is 8 × 6 = 48 square inches, and the diagonal splits it into two equal halves: 24 each. You just discovered the triangle formula!

items.prompt: Let's catch the Shape Shifter's two favorite disguises: a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm, and the sheared rectangle called a parallelogram.

steps.text: Build a rectangle around the triangle: same base 10 cm, same height 6 cm. The rectangle's area is 10 × 6 = 60 cm².
The triangle fills exactly HALF of that rectangle: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 cm². That's the whole formula: A = ½ × base × height.

check.question: Why divide by 2?
options: A triangle covers half of the rectangle built on its base and height
Because a triangle has fewer sides than a rectangle
To make the answer smaller and tidier

steps.text: A parallelogram is a SHEARED rectangle: slice a triangle off one end, slide it to the other end, and it stands up straight again. Nothing gained, nothing lost — A = base × height, no halving.

check.question: A parallelogram has base 7 cm and height 4 cm. Its area is…

steps.text: One trap to dodge: 'height' always means the straight-up distance, never the slanted side. The Shape Shifter LOVES handing you the slant.

items.prompt: Your turn to finish one. A wizard-house banner is a parallelogram with base 8 dm and height 5 dm.

lines: A parallelogram is a sheared rectangle, so A = base × height

items.hint: Sheared rectangles keep their full area — no halving here.
items.explanation: Base × height does it all: 8 × 5 = 40 dm². The shear changes the look, never the area.

items.prompt: A triangular boat sail has base 12 m, height 5 m — and a slanted edge of 13 m trying to distract you.

lines: Pick the TRUE height (ignore the slant!): height = [[5]] m

items.hint: Which of the two measurements points straight up from the base?
items.explanation: The 13 m slant is bait — area uses the straight-up 5 m: ½ × 12 × 5 = 30 m². Spotting the trap is the real skill here.

items.prompt: A round cake pan is 10 cm across. Let's find its circumference AND its area (use π ≈ 3.14).

steps.text: Across = the diameter, d = 10 cm. Circumference is the distance AROUND: C = π × d ≈ 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm.

check.question: A circle is 20 cm across. Its circumference is about…

steps.text: That ratio never changes: around ÷ across ≈ 3.14 for every circle in every realm. So 'times 3.14' turns across into around.
Area uses the RADIUS, half the diameter: r = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm. A = π × r² ≈ 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 cm².
Keep the two apart: C = 31.4 cm is a length around the rim; A = 78.5 cm² counts the squares of cake inside.

check.question: In A = π × r², what does r² mean?

items.prompt: The Duolingo owl's giant circular streak-medal is 30 cm across. Finish finding the trim needed to wrap its rim (use π ≈ 3.14).
items.hint: 'Across' hands you the diameter — circumference is π times that.
items.explanation: C = 3.14 × 30 = 94.2 cm. Around is always about 3.14 times across — that's π's whole job.

items.prompt: Mr. Whiskers naps on a round rug with radius 3 ft. Finish finding the napping area (use π ≈ 3.14).
items.hint: Squaring means the radius multiplies ITSELF.
items.explanation: A = 3.14 × 9 = 28.26 square feet of prime napping territory. r² = 3 × 3, never 3 × 2.

items.prompt: Last one — you drive. A personal pizza is 8 inches ACROSS. Find its area (use π ≈ 3.14).

lines: Area needs the RADIUS first: r = 8 ÷ 2 = [[4]] inches

items.hint: You were handed the diameter. What does the area formula actually ask for?
items.explanation: Halve first, then square: r = 4, so A = 3.14 × 16 = 50.24 in². Catching the diameter-vs-radius switch is exactly the strategy that beats the Shape Shifter.

items.prompt: Two straight yarn strands cross, making an X. One angle of the X measures 62°. What is the angle directly opposite it?
options: 118° — angles across an X make a straight line
28° — angles across an X add up to 90°
It cannot be found without a protractor
items.hint: Opposite angles at a crossing are called vertical angles — what's their famous property?
items.explanation: Vertical angles are mirror twins: always equal, so it's 62°. (The 118° lives NEXT to it, sharing the straight line.)

items.prompt: A parallelogram-shaped sticker has base 9 cm and height 4 cm. What is its area in cm²?
items.hint: A parallelogram is a sheared rectangle — same area rule, no halving.
items.explanation: Base × height: 9 × 4 = 36 cm². Shearing never spills a single square.

items.prompt: The realm's L-shaped courtyard is drawn on a meter grid. Split it into rectangles and add them up: total area in m²?
items.hint: Slice the L into two rectangles — a wide one and a tall one — and sum them.
items.explanation: 6 × 3 = 18 and 3 × 4 = 12, so the courtyard is 18 + 12 = 30 m². Decomposing beats memorizing!

items.prompt: Angle partners: complementary angles add to 90°, supplementary angles add to 180°. Fill in both partners of a 25° angle.
items.hint: C comes before S in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180.
items.explanation: Complement: 90 − 25 = 65°; supplement: 180 − 25 = 155°. Two subtractions, two named partnerships.

items.prompt: A knitted shawl is a trapezoid: parallel edges 7 dm and 11 dm, height 4 dm. Finish finding its area.

lines: A trapezoid uses the AVERAGE of its two parallel bases: (7 + 11) ÷ 2 = [[9]]

items.hint: Average the two parallel edges first — that turns the trapezoid into an honest rectangle.
items.explanation: Average base 9 dm times height 4 dm gives 36 dm². Averaging the bases is the trapezoid's whole trick.

items.prompt: Amal cuts a triangular felt ear for a cat costume: base 12 cm, height 7 cm. What is its area in cm²?
items.hint: A triangle is half of the rectangle built on its base and height.
items.explanation: ½ × 12 × 7 = 42 cm². Half-a-rectangle thinking strikes again!

items.prompt: In a right triangle, the two acute angles measure x° and (2x + 15)°. Solve for x.
items.hint: All three angles of a triangle total 180° — and one of them here is already 90°.
items.explanation: x + (2x + 15) + 90 = 180, so 3x = 75 and x = 25. Check: 25 + 65 + 90 = 180 ✓ — your equation skills just conquered geometry.

items.prompt: A giant cookie is 10 cm across. Use π ≈ 3.14: what is its circumference, in cm?
items.hint: Across = diameter, and C = π × d.
items.explanation: C = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm. Around is always about 3.14 times across — every circle, every cookie.

items.prompt: A round cat bed has radius 10 cm (use π ≈ 3.14). Match each measure to its value.
items.hint: Diameter doubles the radius; C = π × d; A = π × r². The units whisper clues too.
items.explanation: d = 20, C = 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 cm, A = 3.14 × 100 = 314 cm². Area is the only one wearing square units!

items.prompt: The Shape Shifter's goblin apprentice computed a circle's area. Tap the step where it went wrong.

segments: Problem: area of a circle with radius 5 cm (use π ≈ 3.14)
Step A: the formula is A = π × r²

items.hint: Suspicious: Step C's result is exactly this circle's CIRCUMFERENCE. What does the little ² really command?
items.explanation: Squaring means multiply by ITSELF: r² = 5 × 5 = 25, so A = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 cm². Doubling and squaring are different spells!

items.prompt: The Shape Shifter hides behind a T-shaped wall on a meter grid. Decompose it into rectangles: total area in m²?
items.hint: A T is just a long bar plus a stem — two rectangles in disguise.
items.explanation: Bar: 8 × 2 = 16; stem: 2 × 5 = 10; total 26 m². Every weird shape is rectangles wearing a costume.

items.prompt: A staircase-shaped garden bed sits on a meter grid. Break it into rectangles and total the area in m².
items.hint: Three steps, three rectangles — sum all three.
items.explanation: 7 × 3 = 21, 4 × 2 = 8, 2 × 2 = 4, and 21 + 8 + 4 = 33 m². Slice, multiply, add — works on any staircase.

items.prompt: Three corners of the rectangular Great Stacks library sit at (1, 1), (5, 1), and (1, 4) on the realm map. Tap the fourth corner.
items.hint: A rectangle's opposite sides match: borrow the x from one given corner and the y from another.
items.explanation: The missing corner takes x = 5 and y = 4: (5, 4). Bonus: that makes the library 4 wide and 3 tall — area 12.

items.prompt: Unfold a cube like a cardboard box flattened for recycling. Which net folds back into a perfect cube?
items.hint: Fold each option in your head — every face needs a place, with no overlaps.
items.explanation: The cross of 6 squares folds up perfectly. A straight row or a 2×3 grid overlaps itself, and 5 squares leaves a hole.

items.prompt: A chocolate-bar box is a triangular prism (triangle ends, long rectangular sides). Which net wraps it exactly?
items.hint: Count the solid's faces first: how many ends, how many long sides?
items.explanation: A triangular prism has 2 triangle ends plus 3 rectangle sides — 5 faces total. (4 triangles around a square folds into a pyramid instead!)

items.prompt: Surface area = the total area of ALL the faces (think: wrapping paper). Finish this for a cube with edge 4 cm.
items.hint: Picture the cube's net — count every square it unfolds into.
items.explanation: Six faces of 16 cm² each: 6 × 16 = 96 cm². Nets turn surface area into simple counting.

items.prompt: A mini loaf pan is 4 in long, 3 in wide, and 2½ in deep. How many cubic inches of batter fill it to the brim?
items.hint: Volume of a box = length × width × height — the ½ behaves like any fraction.
items.explanation: 4 × 3 × 2½ = 12 × 2.5 = 30 cubic inches. Fractional edges follow exactly the same rule as whole ones.

items.prompt: Shape Lightning! Quick-fire areas, perimeters, and angle facts.

cards: Triangle has angles 90° and 45° — third angle?

items.hint: Formulas on reflex: ½bh for triangles, average-the-bases for trapezoids.
items.explanation: Fast formula facts free your brain for the legendary multi-step quests.

items.prompt: Legendary: The Knotty Skein yarn shop has an L-shaped floor. The left wall runs 8 m, the bottom wall runs 10 m, the tall section is 4 m wide, and the shorter right section's wall is only 3 m tall. How many m² of carpet cover the whole floor?
items.hint: One measurement is missing — the bottom is 10 m and the tall section claims 4 m of it. Sketch it!
items.explanation: The missing width is 10 − 4 = 6 m, so the floor is 4 × 8 = 32 plus 6 × 3 = 18: 50 m². Hunting the hidden measure first is the legendary move.

items.prompt: Legendary: Amal builds a display case for her K-pop lightstick — a rectangular prism 30 cm long, 20 cm wide, and 10 cm tall. Mirror film for all 6 faces costs 2¢ per cm². What is the total cost, in dollars?
items.hint: The six faces come in 3 matching pairs — find each pair's area, total them, THEN bring in the price.
items.explanation: SA = 2(30×20) + 2(30×10) + 2(20×10) = 1200 + 600 + 400 = 2200 cm², and 2200 × $0.02 = $44. Surface area first, money second — two quests in one.
